reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: The bite is small and often painless, so envenomation may be missed until neurological features appear
The venom contains tetrodotoxin, which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and causes progressive flaccid paralysis
Onset is rapid, with perioral and facial paraesthesiae, then bulbar weakness and ascending paralysis leading to respiratory failure
Consciousness is typically preserved even during complete paralysis, so patients may be aware but unable to move or breathe
There is no antivenom; the priority is early recognition and supportive ventilation until the toxin is cleared
First aid with pressure immobilisation is appropriate to delay systemic spread of this neurotoxic venom
Complete recovery is expected if effective ventilation is maintained through the period of paralysis
reference.pathophysiology: Blue-ringed octopuses (Hapalochlaena) secrete saliva containing tetrodotoxin, produced by symbiotic bacteria, which is introduced through a small bite. Tetrodotoxin binds voltage-gated sodium channels on nerve and muscle membranes, blocking sodium influx and preventing action potential propagation. This produces a rapidly progressive flaccid paralysis affecting sensory, motor and respiratory function, with respiratory muscle failure being the lethal effect. Because the toxin does not cross the blood-brain barrier appreciably or affect the cortex, consciousness is preserved despite profound paralysis.
additionalDifferentials: Other cause of acute neuromuscular respiratory failure
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on exposure and characteristic paralysis
Continuous respiratory monitoring and serial forced vital capacity
Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases for ventilatory failure
Electrolytes and baseline bloods to exclude alternative causes
redFlags: Perioral or facial paraesthesiae progressing to weakness
Bulbar dysfunction or difficulty speaking and swallowing
Falling respiratory effort or oxygen saturation
Preserved awareness with inability to move, indicating impending respiratory arrest
reference.prognosis: The outcome depends entirely on airway and ventilatory support; with timely and sustained ventilation through the paralytic phase, patients recover fully, whereas untreated respiratory failure is rapidly fatal.
pitfalls: Dismissing a painless bite and failing to anticipate rapid paralysis
Assuming loss of movement means loss of awareness, leading to inadequate reassurance and analgesia/sedation
Delaying airway support until respiratory arrest occurs
Searching for an antivenom that does not exist instead of prioritising supportive ventilation
management: Immediate pressure-immobilisation first aid of the bitten limb to delay systemic spread of the neurotoxin
Airway protection and mechanical ventilation as the life-saving mainstay, maintained throughout the flaccid paralysis until tetrodotoxin clears, as there is no antivenom
Continuous respiratory monitoring, pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring in a critical care setting
Sedation and analgesia as needed, recognising that consciousness and awareness are preserved despite complete paralysis
Local wound care and supportive haemodynamic and electrolyte management
Early critical-care retrieval and consultation with a clinical toxicology or poisons service, with full recovery expected once the patient is ventilated through the paralytic phase
